newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Food health fears promote demand for organic produce.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Food health fears promote demand for organic produce.

text.p: Europe's market for organic food is booming. Consumer interest is increasing and demand far outstrips supply, say government officials and analysts of the food retail business.

Once viewed as a fad, organic farming is now "becoming a mainstream option" said Patrick Holden, director of the Soil Association, a British lobby group for the practice of agriculture without chemical fertiliser and pesticides.

Britain is a prime target for advocates of organic farm methods because, among European nations, it has been a trailblazer since World War Two in developing intensive, high-tech farming on a wide scale.
It has also recently made news for food health scares, like the alert over mad cow disease, a brain-wasting cattle disease officially known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy, or BSE.
Scientists say BSE may be linked with its deadly human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, and could possibly be transmitted by people eating infected beef.
Infected meat and bone meal mixed into cattle and sheep feed is believed to be the main cause of BSE, which has killed more than 165,000 cattle, mostly in Britain, in the past 10 years.
Lobbyists say the risk of cattle contracting mad cow disease is much lower with organic farming methods.
A FAST-GROWING MARKET
The market in Britain for organic food -- although still modest -- has expanded dramatically, by around 20 percent a year since the mid-1980s, with demand jumping in reaction to the food scares.
According to the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales, the British market rose in value from 40 million pounds ($67 million) in 1987 to more than 150 million ($251 million) in 1994.
At the same time, pressure is building on retailers to offer more organic produce.
"People are far more interested to know exactly what it is they are eating," said a spokeswoman for big retail chain Sainsbury Plc.

"People are frustrated because they cannot get a continuity of supply of organic fruit and vegetables," said a spokesperson for Safeway Plc which says it was the first big British retailer to stock organic goods back in 1981.

Simon Brenman, manager at the Ministry of Agriculture's Organic Conversion Helpline Service said: "The bottom line is that there is a grossly under-supplied market for organic produce in the UK with demand growing every day."
Seventy percent of Britain's organic produce is now imported from other European countries.
"Demand for organic produce far outstrips what we are able to produce in the UK at the moment," said Philip Prideaux of the Soil Association.
SUPPLY INCREASING TO MEET DEMAND
But British farmers have recognised the viability of producing organic food, for which there is a ready domestic market and high premiums.
"In the first two months of this year there has been a 30 percent increase in the amount of land entering for conversion, " said Prideaux.
Organic farming is big business in other European countries. In Austria 200,000 hectares (494,000 Acres) are organically farmed, compared to only 49,000 in Britain.
The Austrian government firmly backs environment-friendly farming techniques, and in 1995 more than 10,000 Austrian farms were in conversion.
"Organic farming is big business now and will be in the future," said a spokesperson from the Euro de Commerce, which represents European retailers.
CALLS FOR GOVERNMENT SUBSIDIES TO BRING DOWN PRICES

Lack of government support is a familiar complaint among British farmers considering converting to organic farming methods, although some hope that the election in May of a new Labour Party government, keen to burnish its "green" credentials, may be a step forward.
Before the Soil Association will accredit British land as officially organic, it must be given two years for all traces of chemicals to disappear.
At present the transition is a risk "that some farmers are unable to take," said Pete Riley of environmentalist lobby group Friends of the Earth.

A spokesperson from the British Department of Agriculture said the government was committed to organic farming," and is "keen to look at the aid rates" offered as encouragement for the two-year bridge period.

Recognising that the higher price of organic produce is a deterrent to some customers, another British supermarket chain, Tesco, has brought down the price of its organic lines to match the prices of their conventional counterparts.
"The result has been overwhelming," said a spokesman, "increasing massively the volume that we've sold."
The present trend towards organic food is illustrated by the situation in Safeways.
"Interest is spreading to other commodity groups such as organic baked beans, because people cannot get continuity of supply on fruit and vegetables," said a spokesman.
